title: The Apocalypse, again
tomorrow: violet, white, green, red: why does a church keep changing colors?

segments.voice: Paul told a feuding church that charity never falleth away. Today, the book that tells how everything else ends.

Disaster movies end in the dust: a skyline in ruins, a few survivors squinting at the sky. The Apocalypse looks like it's heading there too. A dragon, beasts, plagues, a great city falling. Then, near the very end, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "And he that sat on the throne, said: Behold, I make all things new." Not all new things. All things, new.
screen: `A SKYLINE IN RUINS.` → `A DRAGON, BEASTS, PLAGUES.` → `BEHOLD, I MAKE ALL THINGS NEW.`

segments.voice: So what is this book about: the end of time, or right now? Catholic readers lean both ways, and each side has a strong case. Some read it first as a book of the last things. History is going somewhere. Evil doesn't get the final word, and one day God will wipe away every tear and make a new heaven and a new earth. On that reading, the book is a promise about the future, and its hope is something to wait for. Others read it first as a letter to its own day. It opens with messages to seven real churches, under pressure, some of them tired, some compromised. Its beasts point to the powers those churches were facing. And its scenes of heaven, crowds singing holy, holy, holy around the throne and the Lamb, sound like worship, the cry that still echoes at every Mass. On that reading, the new creation has already begun, and Catholics step into it at the altar. The Church keeps both on the table. Something to tell a friend tonight: the book's first word in Greek is apokalypsis, and the Douay translates it revelation, an unveiling. The book's own name for itself isn't doom. It's a curtain pulled back. And behind it, all things new.
screen: `THE END OF TIME, OR RIGHT NOW?` · `A PROMISE FOR THE FUTURE.` · `A LETTER TO SEVEN CHURCHES.` · `A CURTAIN PULLED BACK.` · then, large: `ALL THINGS NEW.`

segments.voice: Write down one thing that needs making new: a friendship, a street, a habit, a part of you. Under it, write the words behold, I make all things new. Sit with the page through the sit, hoping for that one thing, and for nothing bigger.
The Apocalypse. The Bible's last book, a revelation, an unveiling, ending with God making all things new.
Your line: all things new. Not new things; the old ones, renewed and made whole. Talk tomorrow.
